claim: Golgi cells are the principal inhibitory neurons at the input stage of the cerebellum.
source: Golgi cells are the principal inhibitory neurons at the input stage of the cerebellum, providing feedforward and feedback inhibition through mossy fiber and parallel fiber synapses.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract and is established knowledge about cerebellar circuitry.

claim: Golgi cells provide feedforward and feedback inhibition through mossy fiber and parallel fiber synapses.
source: Golgi cells are the principal inhibitory neurons at the input stage of the cerebellum, providing feedforward and feedback inhibition through mossy fiber and parallel fiber synapses.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and represents established knowledge about Golgi cell connectivity.

claim: In vivo studies have shown that Golgi cell activity is regulated by climbing fiber stimulation.
source: In vivo studies have shown that Golgi cell activity is regulated by climbing fiber stimulation, yet there is little functional or anatomical evidence for synapses between climbing fibers and Golgi cells.
evidence: This claim references prior in vivo studies, supported by citations elsewhere in the manuscript.

claim: There is little functional or anatomical evidence for synapses between climbing fibers and Golgi cells.
source: In vivo studies have shown that Golgi cell activity is regulated by climbing fiber stimulation, yet there is little functional or anatomical evidence for synapses between climbing fibers and Golgi cells.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to anatomical studies in the manuscript.

claim: Glutamate released from climbing fibers activates ionotropic and metabotropic receptors on Golgi cells through spillover-mediated transmission.
source: Here, we show that glutamate released from climbing fibers activates ionotropic and metabotropic receptors on Golgi cells through spillover-mediated transmission.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data presented in the results section.

claim: The interplay of excitatory and inhibitory conductances provides flexible control over Golgi cell spiking.
source: The interplay of excitatory and inhibitory conductances provides flexible control over Golgi cell spiking, allowing either excitation or a biphasic sequence of excitation and inhibition following single climbing fiber stimulation.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data showing different patterns of Golgi cell responses.

claim: Single climbing fiber stimulation can produce either excitation or a biphasic sequence of excitation and inhibition in Golgi cells.
source: The interplay of excitatory and inhibitory conductances provides flexible control over Golgi cell spiking, allowing either excitation or a biphasic sequence of excitation and inhibition following single climbing fiber stimulation.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing heterogeneous Golgi cell responses to CF stimulation.

claim: Climbing fibers exert control over inhibition at both the input and output layers of the cerebellar cortex.
source: Together with prior studies of spillover transmission to molecular layer interneurons, these results reveal that climbing fibers exert control over inhibition at both the input and output layers of the cerebellar cortex.
evidence: This conclusion integrates current findings with prior studies on molecular layer interneurons.

claim: Monoamine neurotransmitters and GABA can signal through volume transmission.
source: Since monoamine neurotransmitters and GABA can signal through volume transmission (Fuxe and Agnati, 1991; Overstreet-Wadiche and McBain, 2015), functional connectivity is not strictly synonymous with anatomical connectivity.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work on volume transmission.

claim: Functional connectivity is not strictly synonymous with anatomical connectivity.
source: Since monoamine neurotransmitters and GABA can signal through volume transmission (Fuxe and Agnati, 1991; Overstreet-Wadiche and McBain, 2015), functional connectivity is not strictly synonymous with anatomical connectivity.
evidence: This is inferred from the existence of volume transmission mechanisms.

claim: Glutamate is tightly limited to the synapse by diffusion and reuptake by glutamate transporters.
source: Yet most excitatory neurotransmission is mediated by the fast neurotransmitter glutamate that is tightly limited to the synapse by diffusion and reuptake by glutamate transporters (Wadiche and Jahr, 2005; Tzingounis and Wadiche, 2007).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: At some synapses glutamate can spill out of the synaptic cleft at sufficient levels to activate nearby receptors.
source: Though this argues that anatomical connectivity faithfully represents excitatory circuits, at some synapses glutamate can spill out of the synaptic cleft at sufficient levels to activate nearby receptors (Asztely et al., 1997; Isaacson, 1999; Chalifoux and Carter, 2011; Szmajda and Devries, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior work on glutamate spillover.

claim: Spillover has been studied extensively at cerebellar synapses.
source: This process, termed spillover, has been studied extensively at cerebellar synapses, where it augments conventional point-to-point synaptic transmission between neurons and enables glutamate signaling to Bergmann glia (Bergles et al., 1997; Linden, 1997; Carter and Regehr, 2000; Mitchell and Silver, 2000b; DiGregorio et al., 2002; Mitchell and Lee, 2011; Tsai et al., 2012; Coddington et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by extensive citations to prior work.

claim: Spillover augments conventional point-to-point synaptic transmission between neurons in the cerebellum.
source: This process, termed spillover, has been studied extensively at cerebellar synapses, where it augments conventional point-to-point synaptic transmission between neurons and enables glutamate signaling to Bergmann glia (Bergles et al., 1997; Linden, 1997; Carter and Regehr, 2000; Mitchell and Silver, 2000b; DiGregorio et al., 2002; Mitchell and Lee, 2011; Tsai et al., 2012; Coddington et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Spillover enables glutamate signaling to Bergmann glia.
source: This process, termed spillover, has been studied extensively at cerebellar synapses, where it augments conventional point-to-point synaptic transmission between neurons and enables glutamate signaling to Bergmann glia (Bergles et al., 1997; Linden, 1997; Carter and Regehr, 2000; Mitchell and Silver, 2000b; DiGregorio et al., 2002; Mitchell and Lee, 2011; Tsai et al., 2012; Coddington et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Cerebellar climbing fibers establish powerful synapses with Purkinje cells comprised of several hundred anatomically defined release sites.
source: Cerebellar climbing fibers (CFs) establish powerful synapses with Purkinje cells (PCs) comprised of several hundred anatomically defined release sites (Palay and Chan-Palay, 1974).
evidence: This is established anatomical knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Each climbing fiber release site releases multiple vesicles per action potential.
source: Each site releases multiple vesicles per action potential to generate a high glutamate concentration that overwhelms glutamate transporters, resulting in spillover to neighboring molecular layer interneurons (MLIs) in the absence of an anatomical synaptic connection (Palay and Chan-Palay, 1974; Wadiche and Jahr, 2001; Szapiro and Barbour, 2007; Mathews et al., 2012; Coddington et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work on CF transmission.

claim: Climbing fiber release generates a high glutamate concentration that overwhelms glutamate transporters.
source: Each site releases multiple vesicles per action potential to generate a high glutamate concentration that overwhelms glutamate transporters, resulting in spillover to neighboring molecular layer interneurons (MLIs) in the absence of an anatomical synaptic connection (Palay and Chan-Palay, 1974; Wadiche and Jahr, 2001; Szapiro and Barbour, 2007; Mathews et al., 2012; Coddington et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Climbing fiber glutamate spills over to neighboring molecular layer interneurons in the absence of an anatomical synaptic connection.
source: Each site releases multiple vesicles per action potential to generate a high glutamate concentration that overwhelms glutamate transporters, resulting in spillover to neighboring molecular layer interneurons (MLIs) in the absence of an anatomical synaptic connection (Palay and Chan-Palay, 1974; Wadiche and Jahr, 2001; Szapiro and Barbour, 2007; Mathews et al., 2012; Coddington et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The magnitude of spillover-induced AMPA and NMDA receptor-mediated depolarization is sufficient to trigger MLI spiking.
source: Remarkably, the magnitude of spillover-induced AMPA and NMDA receptor-mediated depolarization is sufficient to trigger MLI spiking, and can modulate PC excitability through feed-forward inhibition (Szapiro and Barbour, 2007; Mathews et al., 2012; Coddington et al., 2013; Coddington et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Climbing fiber spillover can modulate Purkinje cell excitability through feed-forward inhibition.
source: Remarkably, the magnitude of spillover-induced AMPA and NMDA receptor-mediated depolarization is sufficient to trigger MLI spiking, and can modulate PC excitability through feed-forward inhibition (Szapiro and Barbour, 2007; Mathews et al., 2012; Coddington et al., 2013; Coddington et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Glutamate spillover signaling from climbing fibers is sufficient to shape network dynamics even in the absence of anatomical connectivity.
source: Thus, glutamate spillover signaling from CFs is sufficient to shape network dynamics even in the absence of anatomical connectivity.
evidence: This is inferred from the prior work on CF-MLI spillover transmission.

claim: Golgi cells are spontaneously active GABAergic interneurons providing the primary source of inhibition to granule cells.
source: GoCs are spontaneously active GABAergic interneurons providing the primary source of inhibition to granule cells.
evidence: This is established knowledge about Golgi cell function.

claim: Early work suggested that climbing fibers innervate Golgi cells.
source: Early work suggested that CFs innervate GoCs (Scheibel and Scheibel, 1954; Marr, 1969), an idea supported by subsequent in vivo studies showing transient suspension of GoC tonic firing following CF stimulation (Schulman and Bloom, 1981; Xu and Edgley, 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to early anatomical studies.

claim: In vivo studies show transient suspension of Golgi cell tonic firing following climbing fiber stimulation.
source: Early work suggested that CFs innervate GoCs (Scheibel and Scheibel, 1954; Marr, 1969), an idea supported by subsequent in vivo studies showing transient suspension of GoC tonic firing following CF stimulation (Schulman and Bloom, 1981; Xu and Edgley, 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to in vivo studies.

claim: A recent study failed to find structural evidence of synaptic contacts between climbing fibers and Golgi cells.
source: However, a recent study failed to find structural evidence of synaptic contacts between CFs and GoCs (Galliano et al., 2013), and it is unclear how synaptic signaling by glutamatergic CFs would suppress GoC activity.
evidence: This is supported by citation to an anatomical study.

claim: Glutamate spillover from climbing fibers controls Golgi cell activity with a distinct temporal profile in comparison to synaptic transmission from mossy fibers and parallel fibers.
source: Here, we show that glutamate spillover from CFs controls GoC activity with a distinct temporal profile in comparison to synaptic transmission from mossy fibers and parallel fibers, and can suppress GoC spiking by mGluR2 activation.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data.

claim: Climbing fiber spillover can suppress Golgi cell spiking by mGluR2 activation.
source: Here, we show that glutamate spillover from CFs controls GoC activity with a distinct temporal profile in comparison to synaptic transmission from mossy fibers and parallel fibers, and can suppress GoC spiking by mGluR2 activation.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data.

claim: Parallel fiber terminals form synapses on apical Golgi cell dendrites that extend into the molecular layer.
source: Parallel fiber (PF) terminals form synapses on apical GoC dendrites that extend into the molecular layer (ML) whereas mossy fiber (MF) terminals establish synapses on basal GoC dendrites in the granule cell layer (Dieudonne, 1998).
evidence: This is established anatomical knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Mossy fiber terminals establish synapses on basal Golgi cell dendrites in the granule cell layer.
source: Parallel fiber (PF) terminals form synapses on apical GoC dendrites that extend into the molecular layer (ML) whereas mossy fiber (MF) terminals establish synapses on basal GoC dendrites in the granule cell layer (Dieudonne, 1998).
evidence: This is established anatomical knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Parallel fiber-evoked EPSCs in Golgi cells have fast kinetics and facilitating paired-pulse ratios.
source: We used focal stimulation in the molecular layer (while blocking GABAergic and glycinergic inhibition with picrotoxin, CGP55845 and strychnine) to trigger EPSCs with fast kinetics (Figures 1Ai, D and E; 137 ± 20 pA; n = 17) and facilitating paired-pulse ratios (Figure 1Ai and F), consistent with PF synapses (Dieudonne, 1998; Beierlein et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1 and citations to prior work.

claim: Mossy fiber-evoked EPSCs in Golgi cells have slightly faster kinetics than parallel fiber EPSCs and no short-term plasticity.
source: Alternatively, focal stimulation in the white matter or granule cell layer yielded EPSCs with slightly faster kinetics (Figures 1Bi, D and E; 124 ± 16 pA; n = 14) and no short-term plasticity (Figure 1Bi and F), consistent with MF inputs (Kanichay and Silver, 2008; Chabrol et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1 and citations to prior work.

claim: Focal stimulation near Purkinje cell soma evoked all-or-none EPSCs in Golgi cells with kinetics slower than either parallel fiber or mossy fiber EPSCs.
source: In marked contrast, focal stimulation near Purkinje cell soma evoked all-or-none EPSCs in GoCs with kinetics slower than either PF- or MF-EPSCs (Figures 1Ci, D and E; 34.3 ± 4.2 pA; n = 11).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1.

claim: Purkinje cell layer-evoked EPSCs in Golgi cells exhibit robust paired-pulse depression.
source: Slow Purkinje cell layer-evoked EPSCs also exhibited robust paired-pulse depression (PPD), unlike PF- and MF-EPSCs (Figure 1Ci and F).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1.

claim: NBQX application equally blocked the response from all three afferent pathways (parallel fiber, mossy fiber, and climbing fiber).
source: NBQX (5 µM) application equally blocked the response from all three afferent pathways, indicating that EPSCs were mediated by AMPARs (PF: inhibition to 8.5 ± 4.2%, MF: 7.0 ± 3.2%, CF: 8.3 ± 0.4%; n = 3–6, p>0.99 for each comparison, ANOVA, data not shown).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data.

claim: EPSCs from parallel fiber, mossy fiber, and climbing fiber stimulation were mediated by AMPARs.
source: NBQX (5 µM) application equally blocked the response from all three afferent pathways, indicating that EPSCs were mediated by AMPARs (PF: inhibition to 8.5 ± 4.2%, MF: 7.0 ± 3.2%, CF: 8.3 ± 0.4%; n = 3–6, p>0.99 for each comparison, ANOVA, data not shown).
evidence: This is inferred from the NBQX blockade data.

claim: The amplitudes of parallel fiber and mossy fiber-evoked EPSCs were unaffected by TBOA.
source: Whereas the amplitudes of PF- and MF-evoked EPSCs were unaffected by TBOA (Figure 1Aii, Bii, and G), the slow Purkinje cell layer-evoked EPSC was significantly potentiated by TBOA (Figure 1Cii and G).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1.

claim: The Purkinje cell layer-evoked EPSC was significantly potentiated by TBOA.
source: Whereas the amplitudes of PF- and MF-evoked EPSCs were unaffected by TBOA (Figure 1Aii, Bii, and G), the slow Purkinje cell layer-evoked EPSC was significantly potentiated by TBOA (Figure 1Cii and G).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1.

claim: TBOA had little effect on the decay of parallel fiber and mossy fiber-evoked EPSCs.
source: While TBOA had little effect on the decay of the PF- and MF-evoked EPSC, the Purkinje cell layer evoked EPSC was robustly prolonged (PF: 106 ± 6%; MF = 111 ± 15%; CF = 257 ± 30%; n = 15, 9, and 11, PF v MF: p>0.99, PF v CF: p<10−4, MF v CF: p<10−4, ANOVA, data not shown).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data.

claim: The Purkinje cell layer evoked EPSC was robustly prolonged by TBOA.
source: While TBOA had little effect on the decay of the PF- and MF-evoked EPSC, the Purkinje cell layer evoked EPSC was robustly prolonged (PF: 106 ± 6%; MF = 111 ± 15%; CF = 257 ± 30%; n = 15, 9, and 11, PF v MF: p>0.99, PF v CF: p<10−4, MF v CF: p<10−4, ANOVA, data not shown).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data.

claim: Single climbing fiber stimulation was sufficient to evoke CPP-sensitive currents in Golgi cells at +40 mV.
source: Finally, we tested whether NMDA receptors sensed glutamate spillover by voltage clamping GoCs at +40 mV by pharmacologically isolating NMDARs. Indeed, single CF-stimulation was sufficient to evoke CPP-sensitive currents suggesting that under depolarizing conditions NMDARs may contribute to CF-evoked responses (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: Under depolarizing conditions NMDARs may contribute to climbing fiber-evoked responses in Golgi cells.
source: Indeed, single CF-stimulation was sufficient to evoke CPP-sensitive currents suggesting that under depolarizing conditions NMDARs may contribute to CF-evoked responses (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is speculated based on the CPP-sensitive currents observed.

claim: The slow kinetics, strong paired-pulse depression and high sensitivity to TBOA establish criteria for distinguishing climbing fiber-mediated spillover from synaptic parallel fiber and mossy fiber-evoked EPSCs.
source: Together these results suggest that the slow Purkinje cell layer-evoked EPSC is a result of CF signaling to GoCs through glutamate spillover transmission. The slow kinetics, strong PPD and high sensitivity to TBOA establish criteria for distinguishing CF-mediated spillover from synaptic PF- and MF-evoked EPSCs.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data comparing the three pathways.

claim: ChR2 expression was evident in subsets of mossy fiber terminals in CRH-ChR2 mice.
source: Because ChR2 expression was also evident in subsets of MF terminals, we isolated CF activation by targeting light to the molecular layer.
evidence: This is an observation from the experiments using CRH-ChR2 mice.

claim: Brief pulses of light generated all-or-none EPSCs onto Golgi cells with amplitudes and strong paired-pulse depression similar to electrical stimulation near Purkinje cells.
source: Brief pulses of light (1–2 ms; 455 nm) generated all-or-none EPSCs onto GoCs with amplitudes and strong PPD similar to electrical stimulation near PCs (Figure 2A inset, Figure 2B, also see Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2.

claim: The kinetics of light-evoked EPSCs were similar to EPSCs evoked by electrical stimulation near Purkinje cells.
source: Furthermore, the kinetics of light-evoked EPSCs were similar to EPSCs evoked by electrical stimulation near PCs (rise: 1.7 ± 0.3 ms, decay: 8.0 ± 0.9 ms; n = 15 and 11, rise p=0.22 and decay p=0.96, unpaired t-tests, not shown), illustrating that ChR2 can be used to evoke CF spillover to GoCs in CRH-ChR2 mice.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data comparing electrical and optogenetic stimulation.

claim: ChR2 can be used to evoke climbing fiber spillover to Golgi cells in CRH-ChR2 mice.
source: Furthermore, the kinetics of light-evoked EPSCs were similar to EPSCs evoked by electrical stimulation near PCs (rise: 1.7 ± 0.3 ms, decay: 8.0 ± 0.9 ms; n = 15 and 11, rise p=0.22 and decay p=0.96, unpaired t-tests, not shown), illustrating that ChR2 can be used to evoke CF spillover to GoCs in CRH-ChR2 mice.
evidence: This is inferred from the similarity of light-evoked and electrically-evoked EPSCs.

claim: The glutamate concentration at the climbing fiber-Purkinje cell synapse and resulting spillover can be modulated through changes in release probability.
source: The glutamate concentration at the CF-PC synapse and resulting spillover can be modulated through changes in release probability (Dittman and Regehr, 1998; Wadiche and Jahr, 2001; Rudolph et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Increasing extracellular calcium from 2.0 to 2.5 mM increased the average climbing fiber-Golgi cell EPSC amplitude while prolonging the EPSC decay without altering the rise-time.
source: Modestly increasing extracellular calcium from 2.0 to 2.5 mM increased the average CF-GoC EPSC amplitude while prolonging the EPSC decay without altering the rise-time.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: The paired-pulse ratio of ChR2-evoked EPSCs was reduced in 2.5 mM calcium.
source: Consistent with the increase in EPSC amplitude resulting from higher release probability, the PPR of ChR2-evoked EPSCs was reduced in 2.5 Ca2+ (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: Increasing calcium concentration did not alter the sensitivity to TBOA.
source: However, increasing calcium concentration did not alter the sensitivity to TBOA (Figure 2—figure supplement 2B), suggesting that the increase in spillover signaling was not sufficient to alter the regulation of the extracellular [glutamate] profile by transporters.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: In a subset of Golgi cells, there was a step-wise increase in current amplitude with increasing light intensity, suggesting recruitment of multiple active climbing fibers.
source: Interestingly, in a subset of GoCs (11 of 23 cells), we found a step-wise increase in current amplitude with increasing light intensity (Figure 2C), suggesting that high intensity light stimulation was sufficient to recruit multiple active CFs (Mathews et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: EPSCs from multiple climbing fibers maintained climbing fiber characteristics including strong paired-pulse depression and slow kinetics.
source: In these cells, EPSCs maintained CF characteristics including strong PPD (0.15 ± 0.03 and 0.09 ± 0.02 for single and multiple CFs, respectively; n = 11, p=0.09 paired t-test) and slow kinetics (rise time: 1.7 ± 0.3 ms and 1.6 ± 0.23 ms; for single and multiple CFs, respectively; n = 11, p=0.79, paired t-test, not shown).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data.

claim: Electrical and optogenetic stimulation evoke similar spillover EPSCs in Golgi cells.
source: Together these data show that electrical and optogenetic stimulation evoke similar spillover EPSCs and that GoCs can sense spillover from multiple CFs.
evidence: This is inferred from the comparison of electrical and optogenetic stimulation data.

claim: Golgi cells can sense spillover from multiple climbing fibers.
source: Together these data show that electrical and optogenetic stimulation evoke similar spillover EPSCs and that GoCs can sense spillover from multiple CFs.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing step-wise increases in EPSC amplitude.

claim: The intrinsic Golgi cell spiking rate was comparable before parallel fiber, mossy fiber or climbing fiber stimulation.
source: The intrinsic GoC spiking rate was comparable before PF, MF or CF stimulation (5.6 ± 0.8 Hz, 5.0 ± 0.6 Hz, 7.1 ± 0.4 Hz; n = 7, 6, and 25, PF v MF: p>0.99, PF v CF: p=0.25, MF v CF: p=0.09, ANOVA).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data.

claim: Parallel fiber stimulation increased the peak action potential probability to 0.36 ± 0.07 within a narrow spike window.
source: PF stimulation increased the peak AP probability to 0.36 ± 0.07 within a narrow spike window (Figure 3D and E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3.

claim: Mossy fiber stimulation increased action potential probability to 0.53 ± 0.09.
source: Similarly, MF stimulation increased AP probability to 0.53 ± 0.09.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3.

claim: Climbing fiber stimulation prompted a modest increase in the peak spike probability within a broader window consistent with the slow kinetics of spillover EPSCs.
source: In contrast, CF stimulation prompted a modest increase in the peak spike probability (Figure 3C and D) within a broader window that is consistent with the slow kinetics of spillover EPSCs (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3.

claim: A similar number of action potentials were added for all stimulated afferents (measured over 40 ms).
source: Despite the distinct peak frequencies and temporal windows, a similar number of APs were added (measured over 40 ms) for all stimulated afferents (Figure 3F).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3F.

claim: All afferent activity is uniformly capable of recruiting Golgi cell spiking but with distinct temporal profiles.
source: Thus, all afferent activity is uniformly capable of recruiting GoC spiking but with distinct temporal profiles.
evidence: This is inferred from the data showing similar numbers of added spikes but different temporal patterns.

claim: TBOA increased the peak spiking probability over 250% following climbing fiber stimulation.
source: TBOA increased the peak spiking probability over 250% as well as increased the time window of spiking, consistent with spillover signaling (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: TBOA increased the time window of spiking following climbing fiber stimulation.
source: TBOA increased the peak spiking probability over 250% as well as increased the time window of spiking, consistent with spillover signaling (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: TBOA reduced Golgi cell action potential probability to approximately 70% of baseline ~200 ms after climbing fiber stimulation.
source: Unexpectedly, TBOA subsequently reduced GoC AP probability to approximately 70% of baseline (Figure 4B, ~200 ms after CF stimulation, arrow).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Climbing fiber stimulation can regulate Golgi cell spiking in a biphasic manner with both the increase and decrease in excitability regulated by glutamate transporters.
source: This suggests that CF stimulation can regulate GoC spiking in a biphasic manner with both the increase and decrease in excitability regulated by glutamate transporters.
evidence: This is inferred from the TBOA effects on both excitation and inhibition.

claim: In Golgi cells classified as pausing cells, climbing fiber stimulation decreased the spike frequency from 6.7 ± 0.6 Hz to 3.3 ± 0.5 Hz for 93 ± 16 ms.
source: In GoCs classified as pausing cells, CF stimulation decreased the spike frequency from 6.7 ± 0.6 Hz to 3.3 ± 0.5 Hz (p<10−4, paired t-test) for 93 ± 16 ms (n = 9 of 18 cells), which was equivalent to a reduction of the AP probability from 0.13 ± 0.01 to 0.07 ± 0.01 (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: The climbing fiber-evoked average spike frequency was correlated with the climbing fiber-EPSC amplitude across all Golgi cells.
source: Not surprisingly, the CF-evoked average spike frequency (over 40 ms post CF-stimulation) was correlated with the CF-EPSC amplitude across all GoCs (Figure 5E, R2 = 0.2; n = 25, p=0.02).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5E.

claim: There was no correlation between the cumulative ratio and the EPSC amplitude.
source: However, we did not find a correlation between the cumulative ratio and the EPSC amplitude (Figure 5F) nor the cumulative ratio and the CF-evoked average spike frequency (Figure 5G).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5F.

claim: There was no correlation between the cumulative ratio and the climbing fiber-evoked average spike frequency.
source: However, we did not find a correlation between the cumulative ratio and the EPSC amplitude (Figure 5F) nor the cumulative ratio and the CF-evoked average spike frequency (Figure 5G).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5G.

claim: Golgi cell pauses did not result from intrinsic mechanisms that dictate the frequency of firing after depolarization.
source: This suggests that GoC pauses did not result from intrinsic mechanisms that dictate the frequency of firing after depolarization, as occurs with PF- and MF-synaptic stimulation (see below).
evidence: This is inferred from the lack of correlation between cumulative ratio and spike frequency.

claim: Golgi cells express mGluR2, a Gi/Go coupled glutamate receptor that reduces excitability by activating inwardly rectifying potassium channels (GIRKs).
source: Alternatively, GoCs express mGluR2, a Gi/Go coupled glutamate receptor that reduces excitability by activating inwardly rectifying potassium channels (GIRKs; Ohishi et al., 1994; Neki et al., 1996; Luján et al., 1997; Nakanishi, 2005).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Climbing fiber-spillover could suppress Golgi cell spiking via mGluR2-mediated GIRK activation.
source: CF-spillover could thus suppress GoC spiking via mGluR2-mediated GIRK activation, as occurs following strong or high frequency PF stimulation (Watanabe and Nakanishi, 2003).
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on known mGluR2 function and citation to prior work.

claim: TBOA increased the initial climbing fiber-evoked spiking probability in Golgi cells showing climbing fiber-induced pauses.
source: In the subset of GoCs showing CF-induced pauses (Figure 6A), TBOA increased the initial CF-evoked spiking probability (Figure 6B and D) as well as enhanced the duration of the subsequent pause period (from 93.3 ± 16 ms to 183 ± 23 ms; n = 9, p=0.01, paired t-test).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6.

claim: TBOA enhanced the duration of the subsequent pause period following climbing fiber stimulation.
source: In the subset of GoCs showing CF-induced pauses (Figure 6A), TBOA increased the initial CF-evoked spiking probability (Figure 6B and D) as well as enhanced the duration of the subsequent pause period (from 93.3 ± 16 ms to 183 ± 23 ms; n = 9, p=0.01, paired t-test).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6.

claim: Inhibition of mGluR2s entirely blocked post-excitation pausing in Golgi cells.
source: Inhibition of mGluR2s entirely blocked post-excitation pausing, returning the GoC spiking to baseline levels (Figure 6C; TBOA + LY341495 = 6.0 ± 0.9 and 6.7 ± 0.5 Hz, respectively; n = 9, p=0.28, paired t-test).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: mGluR2 inhibition did not significantly change the number of action potentials added with climbing fiber-stimulation.
source: Furthermore, mGluR2 inhibition did not significantly change the number APs added with CF-stimulation and resulted in a cumulative ratio comparable to that of non-pause GoCs (0.89 ± 0.04 n = 12 and 0.93 ± 0.06; n = 9, p=0.57, unpaired t-test and Figure 6D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: Climbing fiber-induced pausing results from spillover activation of mGluR2s.
source: Thus, CF-induced pausing results from spillover activation of mGluR2s.
evidence: This is inferred from the LY341495 blockade of pausing.

claim: Climbing fiber stimulation generates a rapid increase in Golgi cell excitability which can be followed by a longer-lasting suppression of spiking.
source: Together, these results demonstrate that CF stimulation generates a rapid increase in GoC excitability which can be followed by a longer-lasting suppression of spiking.
evidence: This is a summary of the experimental findings.

claim: Climbing fiber-induced inhibition happens in the absence of functional inhibitory connections.
source: CF-induced inhibition happens in the absence of functional inhibitory connections, can be unmasked by uptake inhibition, and is dependent upon postsynaptic mGluR2 activation.
evidence: This is supported by the experimental design blocking inhibitory receptors.

claim: Climbing fiber-induced inhibition can be unmasked by uptake inhibition.
source: CF-induced inhibition happens in the absence of functional inhibitory connections, can be unmasked by uptake inhibition, and is dependent upon postsynaptic mGluR2 activation.
evidence: This is supported by the TBOA experiments.

claim: Climbing fiber-induced inhibition is dependent upon postsynaptic mGluR2 activation.
source: CF-induced inhibition happens in the absence of functional inhibitory connections, can be unmasked by uptake inhibition, and is dependent upon postsynaptic mGluR2 activation.
evidence: This is supported by the LY341495 experiments.

claim: There was a linear relationship between the spiking induced by direct current injection and the subsequent Golgi cell spiking suppression suggestive of intrinsic spike resetting.
source: Indeed, we found a linear relationship between the spiking induced by direct current injection and the subsequent GoC spiking suppression suggestive of intrinsic spike resetting (Solinas et al., 2007b; Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2.

claim: Blocking mGluR2 receptors had no effect on pausing following current injection.
source: However, blocking mGluR2 receptors had no effect, whereas blocking mGluR2 receptors selectively abolished the pause following CF stimulation (Figure 6).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2.

claim: Blocking mGluR2 receptors selectively abolished the pause following climbing fiber stimulation.
source: However, blocking mGluR2 receptors had no effect, whereas blocking mGluR2 receptors selectively abolished the pause following CF stimulation (Figure 6).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6.

claim: Climbing fiber-evoked pausing of Golgi cells are not the result of phase resetting mechanisms that regulate pacemaking activity.
source: These results suggest that CF-evoked pausing of GoCs are not the result of phase resetting mechanisms that regulate pacemaking activity.
evidence: This is inferred from the differential effects of mGluR2 blockade on CF-evoked vs. current injection-evoked pausing.

claim: Stimulation of either parallel fiber or mossy fiber afferents generated a biphasic pattern of Golgi cell spiking, with the synaptically-evoked action potentials followed by a rapid and brief suppression of spiking.
source: We next sought to determine the effect of single PF or MF stimuli on GoC firing. Stimulation of either afferent generated a biphasic pattern of GoC spiking, with the synaptically-evoked APs followed by a rapid and brief suppression of spiking (Figure 7A and C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7.

claim: The pattern of parallel fiber and mossy fiber induced spiking was unaffected either by TBOA or TBOA + LY341495.
source: In contrast to CF stimulation, the pattern of PF and MF induced spiking was unaffected either by TBOA or TBOA + LY341495 (Figure 7A–7D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7.

claim: The insensitivity of parallel fiber and mossy fiber spiking to TBOA is consistent with the insensitivity of the parallel fiber and mossy fiber EPSCs to inhibition of glutamate transport.
source: The insensitivity of spiking to TBOA is consistent with the insensitivity of the PF and MF EPSCs to inhibition of glutamate transport (see Figure 1), and suggests that the pause in spiking reflects a resetting of tonic spike rate (or spike synchronization) due to intrinsic mechanisms that set the interspike interval.
evidence: This is inferred from the comparison of EPSC and spiking data.

claim: The pause in spiking following parallel fiber and mossy fiber stimulation reflects a resetting of tonic spike rate due to intrinsic mechanisms that set the interspike interval.
source: The insensitivity of spiking to TBOA is consistent with the insensitivity of the PF and MF EPSCs to inhibition of glutamate transport (see Figure 1), and suggests that the pause in spiking reflects a resetting of tonic spike rate (or spike synchronization) due to intrinsic mechanisms that set the interspike interval.
evidence: This is inferred from the insensitivity to TBOA and mGluR2 blockade.

claim: The parallel fiber and mossy fiber cumulative ratio was correlated with the spike frequency.
source: Supporting this idea, the PF and MF cumulative ratio was correlated with the spike frequency (Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: Both spillover and synaptic signaling modes can trigger biphasic modulation of Golgi cell excitability, but the underlying mechanisms mediating these changes are markedly different.
source: These results highlight further differences in spillover and synaptic signaling to GoCs. Whereas both modes of transmission can trigger biphasic modulation of excitability, the underlying mechanisms mediating these changes are markedly different.
evidence: This is inferred from the differential pharmacological sensitivities of CF vs. PF/MF responses.

claim: The heterogeneity of climbing fiber-evoked responses is not a result of receptor expression, since all the tested Golgi cells had a similar response to the exogenous mGluR2 agonist.
source: These data show that the heterogeneity of CF-evoked responses is not a result of receptor expression, since all the tested GoCs had a similar response to the exogenous mGluR2 agonist.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing all tested GoCs responded to DCG-IV.

claim: Golgi cells with a large climbing fiber-evoked LY341495-sensitive current exhibited a robust pause following climbing fiber stimulation.
source: As expected, GoCs with a large CF-evoked LY341495-sensitive current exhibited a robust pause following CF stimulation whereas GoCs with a small or undetectable CF-evoked LY341495-sensitive current did not exhibit pausing behavior (Figure 9A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 9A.

claim: Golgi cells with a small or undetectable climbing fiber-evoked LY341495-sensitive current did not exhibit pausing behavior.
source: As expected, GoCs with a large CF-evoked LY341495-sensitive current exhibited a robust pause following CF stimulation whereas GoCs with a small or undetectable CF-evoked LY341495-sensitive current did not exhibit pausing behavior (Figure 9A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 9A.

claim: Across nine Golgi cells there was a correlation between the LY341495-sensitive charge and the cumulative ratio.
source: Across nine GoCs there was a correlation between the LY341495-sensitive charge and the cumulative ratio, further confirming that CF-evoked pausing results from mGluR activation (Figure 9B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 9B.

claim: The subcellular location of spillover signaling to Golgi cells, rather than differences in receptor expression give rise to the observed response heterogeneity.
source: Altogether, these results suggest that the subcellular location of spillover signaling to GoCs, rather than differences in receptor expression give rise to the observed response heterogeneity.
evidence: This is inferred from the uniform mGluR2 expression but variable CF-evoked mGluR2 currents.

claim: Cerebellar climbing fibers signal to Golgi cells by glutamate spillover.
source: Here, we show that cerebellar CFs signal to GoCs by glutamate spillover.
evidence: This is the primary conclusion of the study supported by all experimental data.

claim: Spillover generates direct excitation through activation of AMPARs in Golgi cells.
source: Spillover generates direct excitation through activation of AMPARs, as well as inhibition through activation of mGluRs.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing NBQX-sensitive EPSCs.

claim: Spillover generates inhibition through activation of mGluRs in Golgi cells.
source: Spillover generates direct excitation through activation of AMPARs, as well as inhibition through activation of mGluRs.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing LY341495-sensitive pausing.

claim: The ability of glutamate spillover to inhibit Golgi cell firing suggests that mGluR-mediated inhibition may contribute to the transient pauses in Golgi cell tonic firing reported in vivo by stimulation of the inferior olive.
source: The ability of glutamate spillover to inhibit GoC firing suggests that mGluR-mediated inhibition may contribute to the transient pauses in GoC tonic firing reported in vivo by stimulation of the inferior olive (Schulman and Bloom, 1981; Xu and Edgley, 2008).
evidence: This is speculation based on the current findings and prior in vivo observations.

claim: Antagonizing the mGluR2 receptor blocks the pause in Golgi cell firing conferred by climbing fiber spillover.
source: We show that antagonizing the mGluR2 receptor blocks the pause in GoC firing conferred by CF spillover, further supporting the importance of mGluR2 inhibition of GoC activity seen in vivo (Holtzman et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data with LY341495.

claim: Climbing fibers were suggested to innervate Golgi cells via thin collateral branches.
source: Whereas CFs were suggested to innervate GoCs via thin collateral branches (Shinoda et al., 2000), recent work failed to find evidence for anatomical synaptic contacts between CFs and GoCs (Galliano et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior anatomical work.

claim: Recent work failed to find evidence for anatomical synaptic contacts between climbing fibers and Golgi cells.
source: Whereas CFs were suggested to innervate GoCs via thin collateral branches (Shinoda et al., 2000), recent work failed to find evidence for anatomical synaptic contacts between CFs and GoCs (Galliano et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to recent anatomical work.

claim: Identification of spillover signaling may reconcile conflicting anatomical and functional results showing a lack of synaptic connections between climbing fibers and Golgi cells yet functional consequences of climbing fiber stimulation.
source: Our identification of spillover signaling may reconcile conflicting anatomical and functional results showing a lack of synaptic connections between CFs and GoCs yet functional consequences of CF stimulation.
evidence: This is inferred from the current findings in the context of prior conflicting results.

claim: Golgi cells extend short basal dendrites in the granule cell layer to sample mossy fiber activity.
source: GoCs extend short basal dendrites in the granule cell layer to sample MF activity (Marr, 1969; DiGregorio et al., 2002; Ito, 2006; Kanichay and Silver, 2008) and also extend 2–3 apical dendrites into the molecular layer to receive several thousand PF inputs (Vos et al., 1999; Ito, 2006; Robberechts et al., 2010).
evidence: This is established anatomical knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Golgi cells extend 2–3 apical dendrites into the molecular layer to receive several thousand parallel fiber inputs.
source: GoCs extend short basal dendrites in the granule cell layer to sample MF activity (Marr, 1969; DiGregorio et al., 2002; Ito, 2006; Kanichay and Silver, 2008) and also extend 2–3 apical dendrites into the molecular layer to receive several thousand PF inputs (Vos et al., 1999; Ito, 2006; Robberechts et al., 2010).
evidence: This is established anatomical knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Climbing fiber spillover signaling is expected to occur on apical Golgi cell dendrites in the molecular layer, due to their proximity to climbing fibers that innervate Purkinje cell dendrites.
source: We expect that CF spillover signaling occurs on apical GoC dendrites in the ML, due to their proximity to CFs that innervate PC dendrites.
evidence: This is inferred from the anatomical arrangement of CFs and GoC dendrites.

claim: Spillover signaling may enable integration of synaptic inputs in apical dendrites over a broader time window in contrast to the narrow window of integration of synaptic inputs arising in basal dendrites.
source: Spillover signaling may enable integration of synaptic inputs in apical dendrites over a broader time window in contrast to the narrow window of integration of synaptic inputs arising in basal dendrites.
evidence: This is speculation based on the slow kinetics of spillover transmission.

claim: Single mossy fiber boutons are contacted by ~50–100 granule cell dendrites and usually a single Golgi cell axon.
source: Here, single mossy fiber boutons are contacted by ~50–100 GC dendrites and usually a single GoC axon (Crowley et al., 2009).
evidence: This is established anatomical knowledge supported by citation.

claim: The influence of Golgi cells is facilitated by the complex glomerular geometry that enables GABA released from Golgi cells to spillover to adjacent, non-synaptically coupled granule cells.
source: The influence of GoCs is facilitated by the complex glomerular geometry that enables GABA released from GoCs to spillover to adjacent, non-synaptically coupled GCs (Hamann et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work on GABA spillover.

claim: The extensive ramification of the complex Golgi cell axon allows a single Golgi cell to contact many glomeruli.
source: The extensive ramification of the complex GoC axon also allows a single GoC to contact many glomeruli (Ito, 2006).
evidence: This is established anatomical knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Synaptic activation of Golgi cells generates feedforward phasic inhibition of granule cells.
source: Synaptic activation of GoCs generates feedforward phasic inhibition of GCs, and pacemaker activity contributes to tonic inhibition of GCs (Brickley et al., 1996).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Pacemaker activity of Golgi cells contributes to tonic inhibition of granule cells.
source: Synaptic activation of GoCs generates feedforward phasic inhibition of GCs, and pacemaker activity contributes to tonic inhibition of GCs (Brickley et al., 1996).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Climbing fiber-excitation of Golgi cells has the potential to influence the excitability of thousands of granule cells.
source: Thus CF-excitation of GoCs has the potential to influence the excitability of thousands of GCs.
evidence: This is inferred from the extensive connectivity of GoCs with GCs.

claim: Golgi cells receive GABAergic inhibition from Lugaro cells at a ratio of 10:1 Lugaro cell:Golgi cell.
source: In addition to their glutamatergic inputs, GoCs receive GABAergic inhibition from Lugaro cells (at a ratio of 10:1 LC:GoC; Dieudonné and Dumoulin, 2000; Dumoulin et al., 2001), cerebellar nuclear cells (Ankri et al., 2015), and other GoCs but not MLIs (Dugué et al., 2009; Hull and Regehr, 2012; Szoboszlay et al., 2016).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Golgi cells receive GABAergic inhibition from cerebellar nuclear cells.
source: In addition to their glutamatergic inputs, GoCs receive GABAergic inhibition from Lugaro cells (at a ratio of 10:1 LC:GoC; Dieudonné and Dumoulin, 2000; Dumoulin et al., 2001), cerebellar nuclear cells (Ankri et al., 2015), and other GoCs but not MLIs (Dugué et al., 2009; Hull and Regehr, 2012; Szoboszlay et al., 2016).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Golgi cells receive GABAergic inhibition from other Golgi cells but not molecular layer interneurons.
source: In addition to their glutamatergic inputs, GoCs receive GABAergic inhibition from Lugaro cells (at a ratio of 10:1 LC:GoC; Dieudonné and Dumoulin, 2000; Dumoulin et al., 2001), cerebellar nuclear cells (Ankri et al., 2015), and other GoCs but not MLIs (Dugué et al., 2009; Hull and Regehr, 2012; Szoboszlay et al., 2016).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Reciprocal connections between granule cells and Golgi cells creates a traditional feedback inhibitory loop.
source: Reciprocal connections between GCs and GoCs thus creates a traditional feedback inhibitory loop, that together with feedforward and tonic inhibition, maintain sparse population activity in the GC layer (D'Angelo et al., 2013).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Feedforward, feedback, and tonic inhibition maintain sparse population activity in the granule cell layer.
source: Reciprocal connections between GCs and GoCs thus creates a traditional feedback inhibitory loop, that together with feedforward and tonic inhibition, maintain sparse population activity in the GC layer (D'Angelo et al., 2013).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Reciprocal GABAergic synapses between Golgi cells or connections from Lugaro cells or recurrent Purkinje cell-Golgi cell connections could contribute to climbing fiber-evoked pausing in vivo.
source: We speculate that reciprocal GABAergic synapses between GoCs or connections from Lugaro cells or recurrent PC-GoC connections (Witter et al., 2016) could contribute to CF-evoked pausing in vivo, a possibility that we did not test due to the difficulty of identifying CF-evoked EPSCs in the presence of intact inhibition.
evidence: This is speculation about potential mechanisms in vivo.

claim: Climbing fiber-mediated regulation of Golgi cell spiking displayed distinct temporal properties compared to synaptic signaling from parallel fibers and mossy fibers.
source: We found that CF-mediated regulation of GoC spiking displayed distinct temporal properties compared to synaptic signaling from PF and MFs.
evidence: This is a summary of experimental findings.

claim: Single parallel fiber and mossy fiber stimuli triggered rapid Golgi cell spiking followed by a short-latency pause in tonic firing that was unaffected by mGluR2 antagonism.
source: Single PF and MF stimuli triggered rapid GoC spiking followed by a short-latency pause in tonic firing that was unaffected by mGluR2 antagonism.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7.

claim: The brief pause after parallel fiber and mossy fiber stimulation is likely due to the intrinsic pacemaker firing of Golgi cells that is synchronized across trials.
source: It is likely that this brief pause is due to the intrinsic pacemaker firing of GoCs that is synchronized across trials (Vos et al., 1999; D'Angelo, 2008).
evidence: This is inferred from the insensitivity to mGluR2 blockade and supported by citations.

claim: Golgi cells respond to afferent stimulation with a short burst of spikes that disrupts their intrinsic pacemaker activity.
source: GoCs respond to afferent stimulation with a short burst of spikes that disrupts their intrinsic pacemaker activity (Solinas et al., 2007b, 2007a).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: The pause seen after synaptic stimulation or current injection results from the synchronized reset in the pacemaker activity of the Golgi cell.
source: As a result, the pause seen after synaptic stimulation or current injection results from the synchronized reset in the pacemaker activity of the GoC.
evidence: This is inferred from the intrinsic properties of GoCs and experimental data.

claim: Climbing fiber evoked suppression of Golgi cell spiking depended on mGluR activation rather than intrinsic spike resetting.
source: In contrast, CF evoked suppression of GoC spiking depended on mGluR activation rather than intrinsic spike resetting.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing LY341495 sensitivity.

claim: Both climbing fiber excitation and inhibition were enhanced by application of the glutamate transporter antagonist TBOA.
source: Both CF excitation and inhibition were enhanced by application of the glutamate transporter antagonist TBOA, but suppression of CF spiking was selectively blocked by mGluR2 antagonism, suggesting suppression results from mGluR-induced inhibition, similar to PF burst stimulation that activates postsynaptic mGluR2 on GoCs (Watanabe and Nakanishi, 2003; Nakanishi, 2005).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data with TBOA.

claim: Suppression of climbing fiber spiking was selectively blocked by mGluR2 antagonism.
source: Both CF excitation and inhibition were enhanced by application of the glutamate transporter antagonist TBOA, but suppression of CF spiking was selectively blocked by mGluR2 antagonism, suggesting suppression results from mGluR-induced inhibition, similar to PF burst stimulation that activates postsynaptic mGluR2 on GoCs (Watanabe and Nakanishi, 2003; Nakanishi, 2005).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data with LY341495.

claim: Suppression of climbing fiber-evoked Golgi cell spiking results from mGluR-induced inhibition, similar to parallel fiber burst stimulation that activates postsynaptic mGluR2 on Golgi cells.
source: Both CF excitation and inhibition were enhanced by application of the glutamate transporter antagonist TBOA, but suppression of CF spiking was selectively blocked by mGluR2 antagonism, suggesting suppression results from mGluR-induced inhibition, similar to PF burst stimulation that activates postsynaptic mGluR2 on GoCs (Watanabe and Nakanishi, 2003; Nakanishi, 2005).
evidence: This is inferred from the pharmacological data and supported by citations.

claim: In the intact brain, multiple active climbing fibers may provide spillover to Golgi cells to produce a response under physiological conditions.
source: In the intact brain, multiple active CFs may provide spillover to GoCs to produce a response under physiological conditions.
evidence: This is speculation about physiological conditions based on the experimental findings.

claim: Spillover dependent mGluR-mediated inhibition may augment feedforward GABAergic synaptic inhibition imposed by other Golgi cells and Lugaro cells.
source: In addition, spillover dependent mGluR-mediated inhibition may augment feedforward GABAergic synaptic inhibition imposed by other GoCs and Lugaro cells, although these possibilities remain to be tested.
evidence: This is speculation about potential interactions with other inhibitory mechanisms.

claim: mGluR2 is randomly distributed across the entire somatodendritic domain and axon of Golgi cells.
source: Unlike mGluR1/5 subunits that preferentially localize near excitatory synapses, mGluR2 is randomly distributed across the entire somatodendritic domain and axon of GoCs (Luján et al., 1997).
evidence: This is established anatomical knowledge supported by citation.

claim: The preferential activation of mGluR2 by single climbing fiber stimuli likely reflects the accessibility of spillover glutamate to reach sufficiently large regions of extrasynaptic Golgi cell membranes to recruit detectable mGluR2-mediated GIRK activation.
source: The preferential activation of mGluR2 by single CF stimuli likely reflects the accessibility of spillover glutamate to reach sufficiently large regions of extrasynaptic GoC membranes to recruit detectable mGluR2-mediated GIRK activation.
evidence: This is inferred from the distribution of mGluR2 and the nature of spillover transmission.

claim: Spillover actions are largely regulated by glutamate clearance in the extracellular space and the proximity of postsynaptic receptors to the release sites.
source: Because spillover is not confined to an anatomical post-synaptic site, its actions are largely regulated by glutamate clearance in the extracellular space and the proximity of postsynaptic receptors to the release sites.
evidence: This is established knowledge about spillover transmission.

claim: Transport blockade enhances the duration of the mGluR2-mediated pause.
source: Our results showing that transport blockade enhances the duration of the mGluR2-mediated pause are consistent with this idea.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data with TBOA.

claim: Glutamate release at parallel fiber and mossy fiber synapses is likely constrained to peri-synaptic regions by a high density of glutamate transporters at excitatory synapses.
source: In contrast, glutamate release at PF and MF synapses is likely constrained to peri-synaptic regions by a high density of glutamate transporters at excitatory synapses, such that extrasynaptic mGluR2 activation is controlled by the strength and duration of synaptic stimulation (Watanabe and Nakanishi, 2003).
evidence: This is inferred from the insensitivity of PF/MF EPSCs to TBOA and supported by citation.

claim: Extrasynaptic mGluR2 activation at parallel fiber and mossy fiber synapses is controlled by the strength and duration of synaptic stimulation.
source: In contrast, glutamate release at PF and MF synapses is likely constrained to peri-synaptic regions by a high density of glutamate transporters at excitatory synapses, such that extrasynaptic mGluR2 activation is controlled by the strength and duration of synaptic stimulation (Watanabe and Nakanishi, 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Glutamate released by single parallel fiber and mossy fiber stimuli was insufficient to activate mGluR2-mediated inhibition, even when glutamate transporters are blocked.
source: Our results confirm that glutamate released by single PF and MF stimuli was insufficient to activate mGluR2-mediated inhibition, even when glutamate transporters are blocked.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing no effect of LY341495 on PF/MF-evoked pausing.

claim: Golgi cells in vivo do not show excitation but exclusively show a pause in firing in response to climbing fiber stimulation.
source: Golgi cells in vivo do not show excitation but exclusively show a pause in firing in response to climbing fiber stimulation (Xu and Edgley, 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citation to in vivo studies.

claim: Differences in experimental approaches between in vivo and in vitro studies may contribute to the discrepancy in outcomes regarding Golgi cell responses to climbing fiber stimulation.
source: It is possible that differences in experimental approaches between in vivo and in vitro studies contribute to this discrepancy in outcomes.
evidence: This is speculation about the source of discrepancies.

claim: The discrepancy between in vivo and in vitro results reflects the difference in the probability of identifying a 'paired' recording between a particular climbing fiber and Golgi cell in the two preparations.
source: We speculate that the discrepancy between in vivo and in vitro results reflects the difference in the probability of identifying a 'paired' recording between a particular CF and GoC in the two preparations.
evidence: This is speculation about methodological differences.

claim: Climbing fibers can generate a range of Golgi cell responses including excitation only, biphasic excitation-inhibition and inhibition only, depending on the complement of glutamate receptors responding to spillover.
source: We expect that CFs can generate a range of GoC responses including excitation only, biphasic excitation-inhibition and inhibition only, depending on the complement of glutamate receptors responding to spillover.
evidence: This is speculation based on the experimental findings.

claim: mGluRs have a higher affinity for glutamate than AMPARs.
source: Since mGluRs have a higher affinity for glutamate than AMPARs (Malherbe et al., 2001; Traynelis et al., 2010), it is possible that most GoCs in vivo exhibit solely an inhibitory response, but due to our selection criteria for confirming the CF source of glutamate, all of our GoC recordings have AMPA receptor components that will undoubtedly cause excitation.
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Most Golgi cells in vivo may exhibit solely an inhibitory response to climbing fiber stimulation.
source: Since mGluRs have a higher affinity for glutamate than AMPARs (Malherbe et al., 2001; Traynelis et al., 2010), it is possible that most GoCs in vivo exhibit solely an inhibitory response, but due to our selection criteria for confirming the CF source of glutamate, all of our GoC recordings have AMPA receptor components that will undoubtedly cause excitation.
evidence: This is speculation based on receptor affinities and experimental selection criteria.

claim: Golgi cells are responsible for regulating the responsiveness of granule cells to mossy fiber afferent activity and thus setting the tone of information flow through the cerebellar cortex.
source: GoCs are responsible for regulating the responsiveness of GCs to MF afferent activity and thus setting the tone of information flow through the cerebellar cortex.
evidence: This is established knowledge about GoC function.

claim: The activity of Golgi cells sets the firing threshold as well as controls the timing of granule cell firing and subsequent information transfer to Purkinje cells.
source: The activity of GoCs sets the firing threshold as well as controls the timing of GC firing and subsequent information transfer to Purkinje cells (Gabbiani et al., 1994; De Schutter et al., 2000; Vos et al., 2000).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Tonic and spillover inhibition from Golgi cells play a large role in determining the number of granule cells able to respond to a given mossy fiber input.
source: Tonic and spillover inhibition from GoCs play a large role in determining the number of GCs able to respond to a given MF input (Brickley et al., 1996; Rossi et al., 2003; Duguid et al., 2012), which in turn helps generate a sparse representation that is thought to enhance the storage capacity of the cerebellum.
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Sparse representation generated by Golgi cell inhibition is thought to enhance the storage capacity of the cerebellum.
source: Tonic and spillover inhibition from GoCs play a large role in determining the number of GCs able to respond to a given MF input (Brickley et al., 1996; Rossi et al., 2003; Duguid et al., 2012), which in turn helps generate a sparse representation that is thought to enhance the storage capacity of the cerebellum.
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Phasic inhibition generated by parallel fiber and mossy fiber activity serves to synchronize inhibition, and by extension granule cell activity generating center-surround inhibition.
source: Phasic inhibition generated by PF and MF activity serves to synchronize inhibition, and by extension GC activity generating center-surround inhibition (Vos et al., 1999; D'Angelo and De Zeeuw, 2009; Vervaeke et al., 2010).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Climbing fiber input could serve to demarcate groups of Golgi cells depending on the type of response to climbing fiber input to promote spatial filtering of mossy fiber signals.
source: Since GoCs regulate transmission at the mossy fiber-granule cell relay, CF input could serve to demarcate groups of GoCs depending on the type of response to CF input (with or without an mGluR-induced pause) to promote spatial filtering of mossy fiber signals (Mitchell and Silver, 2000a, 2000b, 2003).
evidence: This is speculation based on the heterogeneous GoC responses and supported by citations.

claim: Recent models emphasize the role of the granule cell layer in the timing of motor commands.
source: In addition, recent models have moved away from the granule cell layer being a simple spatial filter to emphasize its role in the timing of motor commands (Yamazaki and Tanaka, 2009; Rössert et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to recent modeling work.

claim: Golgi cells set the time window for granule cell spiking and time is encoded through the sequential activation of populations of granule cells.
source: In this context, GoCs set the time window for GC spiking and time is encoded through the sequential activation of populations of GCs.
evidence: This is based on recent models of cerebellar function.

claim: Disrupting the cerebellar cortical circuit leads to changes in learned response times while failing to abolish the learned response itself.
source: Indeed, results from behavioral assays in combination with lesioning studies have shown that disrupting the cerebellar cortical circuit leads to changes in learned response times while failing to abolish the learned response itself (Perrett et al., 1993; Raymond et al., 1996; Prestori et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to behavioral studies.

claim: Spillover may serve to desynchronize cells within each layer of the cortex to promote efficient learning.
source: In the context of timing, spillover may serve to desynchronize cells within each layer of the cortex to promote efficient learning.
evidence: This is speculation about the functional role of spillover.

claim: Heterogeneity can arise from differential connectivity patterns between granule cells and mossy fibers, as well as by recurrent inhibition from the Golgi cell network which enhances sparse granule cell activity.
source: Heterogeneity can arise from differential connectivity patterns between GCs and mossy fibers, as well as by recurrent inhibition from the GoC network which enhances sparse GC activity.
evidence: This is established knowledge about sources of heterogeneity.

claim: In recent cerebellar models, mGluR2 activity was suggested to increase the dynamic range of granule cell responses while preventing the circuit from entering an erratic state.
source: In recent cerebellar models, mGluR2 activity was suggested to increase the dynamic range of GC responses while preventing the circuit from entering an erratic state (Rössert et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a modeling study.

claim: Heterogeneity in climbing fiber-mediated mGluR activation on Golgi cells could provide as a source of variability in granule cell layer activity.
source: Thus, heterogeneity in CF-mediated mGluR activation on GoCs could provide as a source of variability in GCL activity.
evidence: This is speculation based on the experimental findings and modeling work.

claim: Conjunctive stimulation of climbing fibers and peripheral inputs may lead to LTD at the mossy fiber-granule cell relay and/or plasticity at excitatory Golgi cell synapses.
source: Here, conjunctive stimulation of CFs and peripheral inputs may lead to LTD at the MF-GC relay and/or plasticity at excitatory GoC synapses (Xu and Edgley, 2008; Robberechts et al., 2010).
evidence: This is speculation supported by citations to prior work on plasticity.

claim: Climbing fiber spillover allows local interneuron circuits to monitor input to Purkinje cells and regulate local circuit excitation and inhibition required to refine cerebellar-dependent actions.
source: In the broader context of cerebellar function, it is possible that CF spillover allows local interneuron circuits to monitor input to PCs and regulate local circuit excitation and inhibition required to refine cerebellar-dependent actions.
evidence: This is speculation about the broader functional implications.

claim: In the context of climbing fibers providing an error signal, spillover signal to Golgi cells may relay privileged information at the input stage that is not encoded by mossy fibers.
source: In the context of CFs providing an error signal, spillover signal to GoCs may relay privileged information at the input stage that is not encoded by mossy fibers.
evidence: This is speculation about the functional role of CF spillover.

claim: Climbing fiber spillover may enhance response complexity and regulate signaling through a form of transmission not constrained to synapses.
source: In this manner, CF spillover may enhance response complexity and regulate signaling through a form of transmission not constrained to synapses.
evidence: This is speculation about the functional implications of spillover transmission.
